claims.text: The initially solid Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles are single-phase, kinetically trapped solid solutions.
Using a solid, mixed precursor at moderate synthesis temperatures limits free atomic mobility.
Increasing the number of constituent elements intrinsically promotes a more random or mixed nanoparticle configuration.
A five-element particle can remain more mixed than a binary particle because limited atomic mobility opposes interaction-driven structural preferences.
The highly mixed multielement solid solution suppresses atomic rearrangements during the premelting regime.
Restricted diffusion in the multicomponent solid solution limits elemental segregation during premelting.
High configurational entropy dilutes element-specific ordering and segregation tendencies.
Configurational effects combined with solid-state mobility constraints force the nanoparticle into a nearly uniformly mixed state.
An absence of significant local compositional fluctuations favors sudden collective lattice destabilization rather than gradual surface premelting.
Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu HEA nanoparticles will melt more sharply and abruptly than analogous binary or monometallic nanoparticles.
The HEA nanoparticles will have a higher melting-onset temperature than analogous binary or monometallic nanoparticles.
The HEA nanoparticles will exhibit less surface segregation and fewer gradual premelting features than the comparison particles.
Binary or single-metal nanoparticles generally exhibit gradual surface premelting and pronounced segregation before complete melting under comparable conditions.
The proposed mechanism applies specifically to nanoparticles prepared from solid precursors with restricted atomic mobility.
The proposed mechanism applies under rapid thermal treatment across the premelting-to-melting regime.
Surface-energy differences and particle-size distributions can affect melting temperature and transition abruptness.
